stem: Hideyoshi's construction of Japan's largest castle at Osaka is best understood as...
stimulus: A modern photograph of Osaka Castle's main tower: a white, five-tiered tower with gold ornamentation rising above massive sloping stone walls. Toyotomi Hideyoshi built the original castle beginning in 1583 as the center of a unified Japan; the present tower is a 1931 reconstruction of the historic keep.
options: (A) a deliberate display of power — the castle's unprecedented scale announced that a single authority now ruled a unified Japan.
(B) a defensive refuge built so Hideyoshi could hide from peasant uprisings and from rival warlords in the surrounding countryside.
(C) a trading post designed to draw Portuguese merchants inland from the coast.
(D) a religious monastery where Hideyoshi retired from political life.
explanation: Osaka was the biggest castle Japan had ever seen, raised on the site of the Honganji temple-fortress Hideyoshi's predecessor had destroyed. Its scale was the message: the age of warring daimyo was over, and the new order had one center — Hideyoshi's.

stem: The screen's depiction of Edo Castle towering over the surrounding city most directly reflects which feature of the Tokugawa political order?
stimulus: A 17th-century Japanese folding screen showing a bird's-eye view of Edo: the shogun's great castle complex dominates the city, surrounded by the mansions of daimyo, temples, and townspeople's districts, with gold clouds drifting above.
options: (A) The emperor in Kyoto, not the shogun, controlled Japan's cities in the 1600s.
(B) The shogun's castle-town of Edo was Japan's political center, with daimyo required to keep residences there under the shogun's watchful control.
(C) Edo was an independent merchant republic free of samurai control, governed by an elected council of wealthy townsmen who paid no taxes to the shogun.
(D) The screen shows that Japan had no central government in the 1600s.
explanation: Edo was the bakuhan system's command post: alternate attendance (sankin kotai) forced daimyo to keep households in the shogun's city, and the castle's dominance over the urban landscape — exactly as the screen paints it — made the hierarchy visible.

stem: The Sankore madrasa's fame under Songhai rule is best understood in the context of which of the following?
stimulus: A modern photograph of the Sankore Mosque in Timbuktu: massive mud-brick (adobe) walls, wooden beams protruding from the walls, and a tall pyramidal minaret-like tower topped with ostrich eggs. Under the Songhai Empire (especially Askia Muhammad, r. 1493-1528), its madrasa made Timbuktu a famed center of Islamic learning.
options: (A) The Songhai rulers banned Islam, so the mosque was built carefully in secret by foreign merchants who hid their faith from Askia.
(B) Timbuktu's scholars were entirely isolated from the rest of the Islamic world.
(C) Songhai's control of trans-Saharan trade routes generated the wealth that funded mosques, scholars, and libraries at Timbuktu.
(D) The madrasa taught only European languages to prepare students for trade with Portugal.
explanation: Timbuktu sat where the Niger trade met the Saharan caravan routes: gold and salt duties flowed to the Songhai treasury, and rulers like Askia Muhammad poured wealth into mosques and the scholars' stipends that made the city the 'Athens of Africa.'

stem: The mosque's mud-brick construction and ostrich-egg finials best illustrate which of the following?
stimulus: Detail from the same Sankore Mosque: its walls are made of sun-dried mud bricks (banco), with palm-wood beams (toron) sticking out that serve as scaffolding for the annual re-plastering; the tower is crowned with ostrich eggs.
options: (A) The mosque was built by Egyptian architects using fine imported stone, exactly like the great historic mosques of Cairo and Alexandria.
(B) Mud-brick construction proves the Songhai Empire was too poor to build in stone.
(C) Local builders ignored Islamic tradition entirely when designing the mosque.
(D) West African builders adapted Islamic architecture to local Sudanic materials and traditions, creating a distinctive regional style.
explanation: Sudanic architecture is Islam in a West African idiom: banco brick and toron beams suit the Sahel's climate and materials, while the form — mosque, minaret, mihrab — is Islamic. The ostrich eggs, symbols of fertility and purity, show local symbolism woven into the faith.

stem: The map's depiction of Songhai's territory along the Niger bend, including Timbuktu and Jenne, most directly explains which source of Songhai power?
stimulus: A modern reference map of pre-colonial African states: the Songhai Empire is shown spanning the great bend of the Niger River in West Africa, with the cities of Timbuktu and Jenne-jeno inside its territory; the earlier Mali Empire lies to its west.
options: (A) Songhai's dominance of Atlantic Ocean shipping lanes.
(B) The empire's control of East African coastal ports, from which its dhows sailed across the Indian Ocean to India and Arabia.
(C) Control of the Niger River trade cities and the trans-Saharan routes through them, yielding taxes on gold and salt.
(D) Songhai's conquest of the Mediterranean coast.
explanation: Songhai's empire was a river-and-caravan empire: holding Timbuktu, Jenne, and Gao meant taxing the gold moving north and the salt moving south. The map's Niger-bend footprint is literally the shape of that commercial control.

stem: Askia's grand tomb and his famous hajj are best understood as...
stimulus: A modern photograph of the Tomb of Askia in Gao (Mali): a steep mud-brick pyramid, its walls studded with wooden beams, topped with an ostrich egg. Askia Muhammad (r. 1493-1528), who made the pilgrimage to Mecca, built it as his burial place.
options: (A) proof that Askia rejected Islam and promoted traditional African religions instead.
(B) efforts to legitimize his rule through Islam — presenting himself as a pious Muslim ruler at home and to the wider Islamic world.
(C) a sign that Songhai's rulers had no interest in connections beyond West Africa and deliberately rejected all foreign contacts and ideas.
(D) evidence that the pilgrimage to Mecca was forbidden to West African rulers.
explanation: Askia had seized the throne from Sunni Ali's son; the hajj (1496–97), his Abbasid caliphal recognition, and monumental Islamic building were how a usurper became God's deputy. The tomb in Sudanic style and the Meccan pilgrimage together claim legitimacy at home and abroad.

stem: This image was created and widely distributed by British abolitionists in 1789. Which statement best explains their purpose in circulating it?
stimulus: A 1789 engraving titled 'Description of a Slave Ship.' It shows deck plans and cross-sections of the British slave ship Brookes, with hundreds of small human figures drawn lying shoulder-to-shoulder in the lower decks, plus printed text giving the ship's dimensions and the regulated number of enslaved Africans it could carry.
options: (A) To shock the public with the crowding of enslaved people and build support for abolition
(B) To provide ship captains with instructions for loading cargo more profitably on each voyage
(C) To celebrate British naval engineering and the efficiency of the slave trade
(D) To advertise the ship to merchants seeking to invest in African trade
explanation: The key is (A). The image was produced by the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade as propaganda: by showing exactly how tightly hundreds of captive people were packed into the ship, abolitionists made the cruelty of the Middle Passage visible and concrete to a British public that had never seen it, building moral and political pressure against the trade.

stem: Based on the stowage plan shown, which conclusion about the transatlantic slave trade is best supported?
stimulus: A 1789 engraving titled 'Description of a Slave Ship.' It shows deck plans and cross-sections of the British slave ship Brookes, with hundreds of small human figures drawn lying shoulder-to-shoulder in the lower decks, plus printed text giving the ship's dimensions and the regulated number of enslaved Africans it could carry.
options: (A) Ship owners limited the number of captives carried in order to keep them healthy on the voyage
(B) Enslaved Africans were given individual cabins much like the crew's quarters
(C) Traders raised profit by crowding as many captive people as possible into the space
(D) The British government had already banned the transport of enslaved people by 1789
explanation: The key is (C). The plan shows human bodies fitted into every available inch of deck space, head to foot, in rows. Each enslaved person represented potential profit on arrival in the Americas, so traders had a direct financial incentive to carry the maximum number the ship could hold, even at the cost of terrible suffering and high death rates.

stem: Which statement about the Atlantic economy is best supported by the diagram?
stimulus: A diagram of the Atlantic triangular trade. Labeled arrows show: 'Manufactured goods from Europe e.g. textiles and spirits to Africa'; 'Slaves to America'; 'Sugar, tobacco and cotton to Europe.'
options: (A) African societies exported plantation crops to Europe in exchange for enslaved laborers
(B) Enslaved Africans were sent to the Americas while plantation products flowed to Europe
(C) European manufactured goods were shipped directly to the Americas to supply the plantations
(D) The trading system connected only Europe and Africa, leaving the Americas out entirely
explanation: The key is (B). The diagram's three labeled arrows form a circuit: manufactured goods (textiles, spirits) went from Europe to Africa, enslaved people were carried from Africa to the Americas, and plantation commodities (sugar, tobacco, cotton) returned from the Americas to Europe. Each leg of the triangle depended on the others.

stem: Portuguese mariners in the 1400s learned to sail far southwest into the open Atlantic before turning east to round Africa. The wind pattern shown best explains this practice because
stimulus: A chart of wind regions over the Atlantic Ocean. It labels a broad 'REGION OF THE N.E. TRADE WINDS' blowing across the tropical North Atlantic toward the equator, a band of 'EQUATORIAL CALMS' near the equator, and a 'REGION OF THE S.E. TRADE WINDS' in the tropical South Atlantic.
options: (A) the equatorial calms provided the fastest sailing route along the African coast
(B) the southeast trade winds blew ships directly from Portugal all the way to India
(C) sailors preferred the calm zones because their ships could not sail in any wind at all
(D) ships could ride the steady northeast trade winds southwest across the open Atlantic
explanation: The key is (D). The chart shows the northeast trade winds as a steady belt blowing across the tropical Atlantic toward the southwest. Portuguese sailors (the volta do mar) swung wide into the Atlantic to catch these reliable winds, which carried them past the contrary winds and currents along the African coast, before turning east to round the Cape. Reading the wind belts on the chart is what makes the answer work.

stem: This map best illustrates which development of the period 1450-1750?
stimulus: A Spanish map of the Americas (from a 1601 atlas) showing the Pacific Ocean labeled 'MAR DEL SVR.' A caption reads, in translation: 'Between the two marked meridians lies the navigation and discovery belonging to the Castilians.' A vertical meridian line divides the map.
options: (A) Spain and Portugal claimed exclusive rights to explore and trade in separate zones
(B) Spain abandoned its American empire in order to focus all of its energies on Asian trade
(C) European mapmakers of the period had no knowledge of the Pacific Ocean at all
(D) The pope forbade all Catholic nations from undertaking any overseas exploration
explanation: The key is (A). The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494), building on papal grants, drew a meridian dividing the non-Christian world between Spain and Portugal. This 1601 Spanish map still displays that logic a century later: the marked meridians and the caption assigning 'navigation and discovery' to Castile show the division hardened into official imperial geography.

stem: The chart was secretly copied for an Italian duke, since Portugal treated its charts as state secrets. What does the chart's content reveal about Portuguese priorities around 1500?
stimulus: The Cantino planisphere (1502), a Portuguese manuscript chart. It shows the coasts of Europe, Africa, and South America (Brazil) in green, the sea route around Africa toward India, compass roses, and rhumb lines used for navigation.
options: (A) Portugal was mainly interested in colonizing North America rather than Asia
(B) Portugal had given up on reaching Asia by sea and turned inward to Europe
(C) Portugal sought the Indian Ocean spice trade while also securing Brazil
(D) Portugal freely shared its navigational knowledge with its European rivals
explanation: The key is (C). The chart carefully traces the African coast and the route around it toward India, marking the spice-trade prize, while also painting Brazil's coast in detail (within Portugal's Tordesillas sphere). That combination on one secret chart shows a crown pursuing two goals at once: the Asian spice trade and the South American claim.

stem: Which statement is directly supported by the diagram?
stimulus: A diagram of the Columbian Exchange with labeled arrows. Blue arrows from the Americas to Europe read 'Maize, potatoes, tobacco, beans, squash, peppers, cacao'; blue arrows from the Americas to Africa read 'Cassava, manioc, cacao.' A red arrow from Europe to the Americas reads 'Cattle, horses, pigs, wheat, rye' and is also labeled 'Smallpox.' A yellow arrow from the Americas to Europe reads 'Syphilis,' and a yellow arrow from Africa to the Americas reads 'Malaria, yellow fever.'
options: (A) Wheat was carried from the Americas to Europe in large quantities
(B) Maize and potatoes traveled from the Americas to Europe
(C) Smallpox traveled from Africa to the Americas with enslaved people
(D) Sugar was carried from the Americas to Europe for refining
explanation: The key is (B). The diagram's blue arrows running from the Americas to Europe are explicitly labeled 'Maize, potatoes, tobacco, beans, squash, peppers, cacao.' Answering requires reading the arrow directions and labels rather than guessing from general knowledge.

stem: The disease arrows on the diagram (smallpox from Europe to the Americas; malaria and yellow fever from Africa to the Americas; syphilis from the Americas to Europe) best support which claim?
stimulus: A diagram of the Columbian Exchange with labeled arrows. Blue arrows from the Americas to Europe read 'Maize, potatoes, tobacco, beans, squash, peppers, cacao'; blue arrows from the Americas to Africa read 'Cassava, manioc, cacao.' A red arrow from Europe to the Americas reads 'Cattle, horses, pigs, wheat, rye' and is also labeled 'Smallpox.' A yellow arrow from the Americas to Europe reads 'Syphilis,' and a yellow arrow from Africa to the Americas reads 'Malaria, yellow fever.'
options: (A) American diseases devastated Europe far more than European diseases devastated the Americas
(B) Malaria originated in the Americas and spread to Africa
(C) Disease moved only from Europe to the Americas
(D) The exchange of diseases contributed to catastrophic Native American population decline
explanation: The key is (D). The diagram shows smallpox arriving in the Americas from Europe and malaria/yellow fever arriving from Africa, while only syphilis moves the other way. Native populations had no prior exposure or immunity to these Old World diseases, so the epidemics they caused killed a huge proportion of Indigenous peoples, a demographic catastrophe visible in the one-sided disease arrows.

stem: A historian studying the impact of European contact on Indigenous peoples would value this image most because it
stimulus: A 1577 illustration from Book 12 of the Florentine Codex, a history compiled by Nahua (Aztec) scribes working with a Spanish friar. It shows Mexica smallpox victims lying ill, their bodies covered in sores, while a healer attends to one of them.
options: (A) records the epidemic from the perspective of the Nahua people who suffered it
(B) proves that Spanish friars introduced smallpox to the Americas intentionally
(C) shows that Native healers were able to cure smallpox with traditional medicine
(D) was painted by a Spanish conquistador who personally witnessed the siege of Tenochtitlan
explanation: The key is (A). Most surviving accounts of the conquest-era epidemics were written by Europeans. This image was drawn by Nahua scribes recording their own community's catastrophe, giving historians a rare Indigenous perspective on the epidemic: who fell ill, how caregivers responded, and how the disaster was remembered by its victims.

stem: Based on details in the image, which claim about the smallpox epidemic is best supported?
stimulus: A 1577 illustration from Book 12 of the Florentine Codex, a history compiled by Nahua (Aztec) scribes working with a Spanish friar. It shows Mexica smallpox victims lying ill, their bodies covered in sores, while a healer attends to one of them.
options: (A) Only Spanish soldiers caught the disease, while Native people were immune
(B) The victims shown are recovering from the illness and returning to work
(C) The disease struck many people at once, overwhelming caregivers
(D) The Mexica blamed the epidemic on their own gods and took no action
explanation: The key is (C). The image shows several victims lying ill simultaneously, their bodies covered in pustules, with a single healer attending one of them. Multiple sufferers at once with limited care is exactly what made virgin-soil epidemics so deadly: whole households fell ill together, so there was no one healthy left to nurse the sick or bring food and water.

stem: The labor system shown in the engraving is best identified as
stimulus: A cross-section engraving titled 'A Section of a Silver Mine in Potosi, and the Manner of Working it' (c. 1750). It shows laborers climbing steep ladders inside the mountain carrying baskets of ore on their backs, with a mining town at the mountain's base.
options: (A) the encomienda, the grant of Indigenous tribute and labor to Spanish settlers
(B) the mita, the colonial draft-labor system that supplied workers to the mines
(C) wage labor freely contracted by independent Spanish miners
(D) the repartimiento of enslaved Africans to the silver mines
explanation: The key is (B). The engraving shows Indigenous laborers doing the brutal work of carrying ore up ladders inside the Cerro Rico at Potosi. This was the mita: a colonial draft that required Indigenous communities to send a rotating share of their men to work the mines, adapted from an Inca labor obligation into the engine of Spanish silver production.

stem: The scale of mining shown at Potosi best helps explain which broader development?
stimulus: A cross-section engraving titled 'A Section of a Silver Mine in Potosi, and the Manner of Working it' (c. 1750). It shows laborers climbing steep ladders inside the mountain carrying baskets of ore on their backs, with a mining town at the mountain's base.
options: (A) the abandonment of mining across Spanish America in favor of plantation agriculture
(B) the collapse of trade between Europe and Asia in the 1700s
(C) the end of forced labor in the Spanish colonies by the mid-1700s
(D) Spain's ability to fund its wars and worldwide empire with American silver
explanation: The key is (D). Potosi was the richest silver source in the world; the engraving's cutaway of the honeycombed mountain and its dependent town conveys the industrial scale of extraction. The Spanish crown took a royal fifth of this silver, and the flood of American bullion financed Spain's armies, its bureaucracy, and its purchases of Asian goods, making silver the financial base of the first global empire.

stem: This painting best illustrates which feature of Spanish colonial society?
stimulus: An eighteenth-century Mexican casta painting labeled (in translation) 'From Black and Spaniard comes Mulatto.' It shows a Spanish father, an African mother, and their child in a domestic scene, with the racial labels painted into the composition.
options: (A) a formal social hierarchy that classified people by ancestry and race
(B) the legal equality of all free people in the colonies regardless of ancestry
(C) the absence of African slavery anywhere in New Spain
(D) a legal ban on marriage between people of different backgrounds
explanation: The key is (A). Casta paintings were a whole genre dedicated to labeling the supposed results of racial mixing ('mulatto,' 'mestizo,' and a dozen more). That colonial elites commissioned sets of these paintings shows race and ancestry were treated as an official system for ranking people, with Spaniards at the top.

stem: Compared with the English colonies in North America, the Spanish colonies' production of paintings like this one suggests that Spanish America
stimulus: An eighteenth-century Mexican casta painting labeled (in translation) 'From Black and Spaniard comes Mulatto.' It shows a Spanish father, an African mother, and their child in a domestic scene, with the racial labels painted into the composition.
options: (A) had fewer people of mixed ancestry living in it than the English colonies did
(B) prohibited all social contact between Europeans and Africans
(C) built a more elaborate system for classifying people of mixed ancestry
(D) granted equal legal status to people of all castas under colonial law
explanation: The key is (C). The English colonies never produced a genre of paintings classifying racial mixtures; their racial boundary hardened into a simpler Black/white divide. The existence of entire labeled series of casta paintings shows Spanish America uniquely institutionalized the classification of mixed-ancestry people into named categories tied to social rank.

stem: The lateen sails shown on the model were significant because they
stimulus: A modern museum model of a fifteenth-century Portuguese caravel. The model shows a small, maneuverable hull with lateen (triangular) sails mounted on long yards, and a cross of the Order of Christ painted on the sail.
options: (A) allowed ships to carry more cannon than any earlier vessel had carried
(B) let ships sail closer to the wind, enabling long Atlantic voyages
(C) were copied directly from Chinese junk designs by the Portuguese
(D) made ships slower but more comfortable for passengers on long trips
explanation: The key is (B). Triangular lateen sails could be angled to catch the wind from the side, letting ships tack against headwinds instead of waiting for a following wind. Combined with a sturdy hull, this made it possible to sail the long Atlantic loops (out with the trades, back with the westerlies) that exploration required.

stem: The scene best supports which conclusion about Caribbean plantation economies?
stimulus: An engraving of a Caribbean sugar plantation. Enslaved African laborers cut tall cane with machetes while others bundle the stalks; an ox-drawn cart hauls cane toward a mill with tall chimneys in the background.
options: (A) Plantations relied mainly on European indentured servants during this period
(B) Sugar was grown only for local consumption in the Caribbean
(C) Plantation owners preferred to divide land into small family farms
(D) Sugar production depended on enslaved African labor organized for export
explanation: The key is (D). The engraving shows gangs of enslaved African workers cutting, bundling, and hauling cane to a central mill: an industrial-scale workforce producing a single cash crop. Sugar grown in the Caribbean was shipped to European markets, and the labor demand of the harvest was met overwhelmingly by enslaved Africans.

stem: The mill shown in the background of the engraving helps explain why sugar cultivation led to
stimulus: An engraving of a Caribbean sugar plantation. Enslaved African laborers cut tall cane with machetes while others bundle the stalks; an ox-drawn cart hauls cane toward a mill with tall chimneys in the background.
options: (A) the rise of large plantations built around expensive centralized mills
(B) the decline of slavery, since mills greatly reduced the need for workers
(C) European governments banning the importation of colonial sugar
(D) planters switching from sugar cane to tobacco
explanation: The key is (A). Cut cane spoils quickly and must be crushed, boiled, and refined promptly, which required a costly mill. Only large, well-capitalized plantations could afford the equipment, so sugar pushed land and labor to concentrate in big units worked by enslaved gangs rather than small farms.

stem: The interaction depicted best illustrates which pattern of European-Indigenous relations in North America?
stimulus: A 1777 engraving titled 'Fur traders in Canada.' It shows two European traders, one inspecting a large pelt held up by an Indigenous man carrying a bow, while another Indigenous man sits smoking a long pipe beside a barrel of trade goods.
options: (A) Europeans enslaving Indigenous peoples to work on fur-trapping plantations
(B) Indigenous peoples refusing all trade with Europeans on principle
(C) a commercial partnership in which Europeans depended on Indigenous hunters
(D) French missionaries converting Indigenous peoples to Christianity in the region
explanation: The key is (C). The engraving shows a transaction, not a conquest: the Indigenous man presents the pelt as the seller while the European inspects it as the buyer, with trade goods (the barrel) and relaxed pipe-smoking around them. Europeans could not harvest furs at scale themselves; they depended on Indigenous hunters' skills, territory, and willingness to trade.

stem: Which detail in the engraving best shows Indigenous agency in the fur trade?
stimulus: A 1777 engraving titled 'Fur traders in Canada.' It shows two European traders, one inspecting a large pelt held up by an Indigenous man carrying a bow, while another Indigenous man sits smoking a long pipe beside a barrel of trade goods.
options: (A) The Europeans' large barrel of manufactured goods offered for exchange
(B) The Indigenous trader displaying the pelt for inspection as the seller
(C) The European clothing worn by the two traders
(D) The absence of any written contract in the scene depicted
explanation: The key is (B). Agency means the capacity to act and negotiate. The Indigenous man controls the pelt, displays it, and sets the terms of inspection; the European must evaluate what is offered to him. The seller's posture, not the buyer's, drives the transaction shown.

stem: Because this screen was painted by Japanese artists for Japanese viewers, it is most useful to historians as evidence of
stimulus: A Japanese folding screen (nanban byobu) showing the arrival of a Portuguese 'black ship' (carrack). The great black-hulled ship anchors offshore while Japanese boats ferry cargo and Portuguese merchants in distinctive hats and capes walk ashore carrying chests, observed by Japanese onlookers.
options: (A) Portuguese naval victories over Japan in the 1500s
(B) the Japanese desire to be colonized by Portugal after these visits ended
(C) European artistic techniques being used in Asia
(D) how Japanese observers saw the exotic Portuguese traders from the sea
explanation: The key is (D). The screen centers Japanese eyes: the huge black ship dominates as a wonder, the Portuguese are rendered as strange-looking foreigners ('southern barbarians') in odd clothing, and Japanese figures crowd the shore to watch. It records the encounter from the receiving side, showing Europeans as the exotic outsiders rather than as conquerors.

stem: Details in the screen, such as Japanese boats ferrying the cargo ashore and Japanese onlookers directing the scene while the Portuguese come to them, best support which conclusion about this trade?
stimulus: A Japanese folding screen (nanban byobu) showing the arrival of a Portuguese 'black ship' (carrack). The great black-hulled ship anchors offshore while Japanese boats ferry cargo and Portuguese merchants in distinctive hats and capes walk ashore carrying chests, observed by Japanese onlookers.
options: (A) The Portuguese traded in Japan on terms largely set by the Japanese
(B) Portugal had conquered the Japanese port where the ship had landed by force
(C) Japan depended on Portugal for military protection against China
(D) The Japanese refused to allow any Portuguese to come ashore at all
explanation: The key is (A). The Portuguese do not stride in as masters: their ship waits offshore, Japanese boats handle the cargo, and Japanese figures manage the landing. The visual arrangement shows the visitors operating inside a Japanese-controlled setting, which matches the history: the Portuguese came as supplicants for trade that the Japanese authorities permitted and regulated.

stem: The map best supports which conclusion about the Mexica capital the Spanish encountered?
stimulus: A 1524 printed map of Tenochtitlan, published in Europe with Hernan Cortes's letters. It shows a great city on a lake, ringed by water, with long causeways connecting it to the shore, a walled central temple precinct labeled in Latin, canals, canoes, and dense blocks of buildings.
options: (A) It was a small village made up of temporary huts
(B) It had been abandoned long before the Spanish arrived
(C) It was a large, planned urban center
(D) It was built by the Spanish only after the conquest
explanation: The key is (C). The map shows a city covering the lake with causeways, a grid of canals and streets, dense housing blocks, and a great walled ceremonial precinct at its heart. That is the portrait of a complex, deliberately planned imperial capital, one of the largest cities in the world in 1519, not a primitive settlement.

stem: A historian using this map as evidence about Tenochtitlan should keep in mind that the map
stimulus: A 1524 printed map of Tenochtitlan, published in Europe with Hernan Cortes's letters. It shows a great city on a lake, ringed by water, with long causeways connecting it to the shore, a walled central temple precinct labeled in Latin, canals, canoes, and dense blocks of buildings.
options: (A) was drawn by Mexica priests to record their own history of the city
(B) was produced in Europe to accompany Cortes's reports to the king
(C) shows the city exactly as it had appeared in the year 1325
(D) was banned by the Spanish crown for criticizing the conquest harshly
explanation: The key is (B). The map was printed in Nuremberg to illustrate Cortes's published letters to Charles V, whose favor and funding Cortes needed. A map made to impress a king was likely to emphasize the city's grandeur and riches (justifying the conquest) while rendering it in familiar European visual language, so historians read it as a European representation, not a neutral photograph.

stem: The plan best illustrates which Dutch colonial priority in North America?
stimulus: The Castello Plan of New Amsterdam (1660), a Dutch manuscript map. It shows a compact walled settlement at the tip of Manhattan: a fort, a grid of streets, a canal, a windmill, houses, and warehouses along the waterfront, with ships anchored offshore.
options: (A) converting Indigenous peoples to Christianity as its main goal
(B) establishing large plantation agriculture in the region
(C) mining gold and silver in the surrounding hills
(D) building a fortified commercial outpost for trade
explanation: The key is (D). The plan shows a small walled town organized around its harbor: the fort guards the settlement, warehouses line the waterfront, and ships ride at anchor. Everything serves commerce and its defense. The Dutch West India Company founded New Amsterdam as a trading post for furs and Atlantic commerce, not as a mission, plantation colony, or mining camp.

stem: Unlike the sprawling Spanish colonial cities built around a central plaza and cathedral, New Amsterdam as shown in the plan was organized primarily around
stimulus: The Castello Plan of New Amsterdam (1660), a Dutch manuscript map. It shows a compact walled settlement at the tip of Manhattan: a fort, a grid of streets, a canal, a windmill, houses, and warehouses along the waterfront, with ships anchored offshore.
options: (A) the harbor and warehouses of a settlement designed for commerce
(B) military barracks of a settlement designed primarily for conquest
(C) churches and monasteries of a settlement designed for missions
(D) plantation fields of a settlement designed for farming
explanation: The key is (A). Spanish colonial cities expressed crown and church authority through the plaza-cathedral-palace layout. The Castello Plan shows a different logic: the town's energy faces the water, where warehouses, the canal, and anchored ships dominate. The comparison reveals a settlement whose organizing principle was trade, matching the Dutch commercial empire's priorities versus Spain's imperial-administrative ones.

stem: Given that de Bry never visited the Americas, historians treat images like this one primarily as evidence of
stimulus: A 1593 engraving by Theodor de Bry titled 'Tupinamba cannibals.' It shows Tupinamba people in Brazil roasting human limbs on a wooden grill while others dance and play instruments. De Bry, a Frankfurt engraver and publisher, never traveled to the Americas; he based his images on travelers' accounts.
options: (A) the exact rituals practiced by the Tupinamba in Brazil
(B) Portuguese military victories over the peoples of Brazil
(C) European imaginations and fears about Indigenous peoples
(D) Tupinamba artistic traditions of the sixteenth century
explanation: The key is (C). De Bry assembled his scenes in Frankfurt from secondhand stories, aiming to sell books to thrill-seeking European readers. The lurid grill scene tells us far more about what Europeans imagined, feared, and enjoyed reading about 'savages' than about actual Tupinamba life, making the engraving a window into the European mind.

stem: Which historical question could this engraving best help answer?
stimulus: A 1593 engraving by Theodor de Bry titled 'Tupinamba cannibals.' It shows Tupinamba people in Brazil roasting human limbs on a wooden grill while others dance and play instruments. De Bry, a Frankfurt engraver and publisher, never traveled to the Americas; he based his images on travelers' accounts.
options: (A) What did the spoken Tupinamba language sound like to European visitors?
(B) How did Europeans portray Indigenous Americans to justify conquest?
(C) How many Tupinamba people were living in Brazil in 1593?
(D) What crops did the Tupinamba grow in their villages?
explanation: The key is (B). The engraving is most useful not as a record of Tupinamba life but as a record of European representation: it shows the 'savage cannibal' stereotype that made conquest look like a civilizing mission and that sold de Bry's illustrated volumes. Historians use it to study propaganda and prejudice, not ethnography.

stem: The design features shown in the diagram best reflect which Spanish priority?
stimulus: A 1734 Spanish diagram of a galleon, with labels identifying its parts. The ship has multiple gun decks lined with cannon, high fore- and stern-castles, and a large hull for cargo.
options: (A) speed for outrunning storms on the Pacific crossing
(B) comfort for transporting large numbers of settlers to America safely
(C) a shallow draft suitable for river exploration
(D) protecting valuable silver shipments with heavily armed vessels
explanation: The key is (D). The diagram emphasizes gun decks bristling with cannon alongside a capacious cargo hull: a warship-merchant hybrid. Spanish treasure fleets carried the silver of Potosi and Mexico through waters prowled by pirates and rival navies, so the galleon was designed to fight off attackers while hauling bullion.

stem: Elmina (built by the Portuguese in 1482) best exemplifies the European strategy of
stimulus: A 1668 engraving of Elmina Castle on the coast of West Africa. It shows a massive stone fortress with a church, walls, and cannons overlooking the sea, with a European ship anchored offshore and an African town nearby.
options: (A) building fortified coastal trading posts rather than settler colonies
(B) conquering and directly ruling the African interior kingdoms nearby by force
(C) banning all trade with the African kingdoms
(D) founding plantation colonies along the African coast
explanation: The key is (A). The engraving shows exactly the feitoria model: a powerful but compact coastal fortress with its church and guns, a ship offshore, and an African town beside it rather than a European colony around it. Europeans wanted gold and later captives from African trade networks, and a fortified post secured that commerce without the cost of territorial conquest.

stem: By 1668, when this engraving was made, Elmina had been captured and held by the Dutch for over thirty years. The continued operation of the fort under new ownership best illustrates
stimulus: A 1668 engraving of Elmina Castle on the coast of West Africa. It shows a massive stone fortress with a church, walls, and cannons overlooking the sea, with a European ship anchored offshore and an African town nearby.
options: (A) the end of all European interest in African trade altogether
(B) African kingdoms driving all of the Europeans off the coast entirely by force
(C) the fortified-trade model continuing as rival empires replaced one another
(D) the Dutch shift from trade to large-scale settlement in Africa
explanation: The key is (C). The Portuguese built Elmina; the Dutch seized it in 1637 and ran the same gold and slave trade from the same walls. The 1668 engraving, made under Dutch ownership, shows the fort unchanged in function: what changed was the flag, not the system. Rival empires inherited and continued the fortified-trading-post model.

stem: The building shown was central to which economic development of the 1600s?
stimulus: A 1612 bird's-eye engraving of the Amsterdam stock exchange (Beurs van Hendrick de Keyser). It shows a grand courtyard building crowded with merchants gathered in groups, with galleries and offices around the square.
options: (A) the return to barter economies across Europe
(B) the rise of joint-stock companies and share trading
(C) the banning of overseas investment by the European states
(D) the decline of Amsterdam as a major trading city
explanation: The key is (B). The Amsterdam bourse was the world's first formal stock exchange, where shares of the Dutch East India Company (VOC), founded 1602, were bought and sold. The engraving's crowds of merchants gathered to trade paper shares show the new financial machinery: joint-stock ownership and a public market for it.

stem: Institutions like the one shown best explain how the Dutch were able to
stimulus: A 1612 bird's-eye engraving of the Amsterdam stock exchange (Beurs van Hendrick de Keyser). It shows a grand courtyard building crowded with merchants gathered in groups, with galleries and offices around the square.
options: (A) avoid all financial risk in overseas trading ventures
(B) prevent any other European nation from trading in Asia at all
(C) abolish the transatlantic slave trade entirely
(D) pool capital from many investors to fund expensive voyages
explanation: The key is (D). Outfitting an East Indiaman for a two-year voyage cost a fortune and could end in shipwreck. By selling shares to hundreds of investors and letting them trade those shares at the bourse, the Dutch spread the risk and assembled capital no single merchant could raise, bankrolling the VOC's Asian empire.

stem: The island's design best reflects which Tokugawa policy?
stimulus: A bird's-eye engraving of Dejima, the small fan-shaped artificial island in Nagasaki harbor. It shows Dutch warehouses, residences, and gardens packed onto the island, which is connected to the Japanese mainland by a single guarded bridge.
options: (A) limiting European contact to one supervised port
(B) welcoming Dutch settlers to live throughout Japan
(C) banning all foreign trade with Japan entirely
(D) granting the Dutch territorial colonies within Japan
explanation: The key is (A). After expelling the Portuguese and restricting Christianity, the Tokugawa shogunate confined the Dutch to Dejima, an artificial island that could be watched and sealed. The single guarded bridge in the engraving is the visual proof: trade was permitted but Europeans were physically quarantined from Japanese society.

stem: Compared with the Spanish and Portuguese empires in the Americas, Tokugawa Japan's treatment of the Dutch as shown here demonstrates
stimulus: A bird's-eye engraving of Dejima, the small fan-shaped artificial island in Nagasaki harbor. It shows Dutch warehouses, residences, and gardens packed onto the island, which is connected to the Japanese mainland by a single guarded bridge.
options: (A) that Japan lacked the military power to resist the Europeans at all
(B) that Europeans had no real interest in trading with Japan
(C) that a strong Asian state could set the terms of European trade
(D) that Japan had adopted Christianity as its state religion
explanation: The key is (C). In the Americas, Europeans imposed the terms of contact; in Japan, the shogunate imposed them, penning the Dutch onto a supervised island. The contrast shows European expansion was not irresistible: where a centralized, powerful state existed, Europeans traded as guests under local rules rather than as conquerors.

stem: The map's careful charting of Hudson Bay's rivers and coasts best reflects which British interest?
stimulus: A 1776 British map of Hudson Bay and the surrounding lands. It labels the bay, its rivers, and the northern coastline in detail, with a cartouche celebrating the region's commercial importance.
options: (A) establishing sugar plantations in the north of Canada
(B) securing the fur-trade network of the Hudson's Bay Company
(C) finding gold mines in the Arctic regions
(D) converting the Indigenous peoples of the region to Christianity
explanation: The key is (B). The Hudson's Bay Company, chartered in 1670, built its fur empire on the bay's river systems, which carried pelts from the interior to its coastal posts. A detailed commercial map of those rivers and shores served the fur trade's logistics: locating posts, planning canoe routes, and defending the company's chartered monopoly.

stem: Furs gathered in the region shown on the map were shipped to Europe, where beaver pelts were made into fashionable hats. This best illustrates
stimulus: A 1776 British map of Hudson Bay and the surrounding lands. It labels the bay, its rivers, and the northern coastline in detail, with a cartouche celebrating the region's commercial importance.
options: (A) the self-sufficiency of the colonial economies in North America
(B) the decline of European demand for luxury goods such as furs
(C) Indigenous peoples' rejection of European goods in trade
(D) how colonial extraction of resources fed European markets
explanation: The key is (D). The bay's furs did not stay in North America; they crossed the Atlantic to become hats for European consumers. The map's commercial geography, tied to a distant fashion market, shows the colonial economy's role as a supplier of raw materials to European demand, a core pattern of the Atlantic economy.

stem: The Dutch settlement at the Cape of Good Hope shown here served primarily as
stimulus: A 1683 painting of Table Bay (Cape Town) showing Dutch ships anchored beneath Table Mountain, with small boats ferrying goods and people between the ships and the shore settlement.
options: (A) a station where VOC ships restocked food and water en route to Asia
(B) a penal colony for convicted Dutch criminals
(C) a plantation colony growing spices for the European market
(D) the capital of a large and powerful Dutch settler empire in southern Africa
explanation: The key is (A). The painting shows ships at anchor being serviced by shore boats: the Cape's purpose was logistical. Founded in 1652, the station grew fresh food and supplied water so VOC crews could survive the long Indian Ocean leg, as the anchored men-of-war and ferry boats in the image suggest.

stem: The Dutch established the station shown because the voyage between Europe and Asia
stimulus: A 1683 painting of Table Bay (Cape Town) showing Dutch ships anchored beneath Table Mountain, with small boats ferrying goods and people between the ships and the shore settlement.
options: (A) was too short to need any stops along the way
(B) passed through ocean waters with no wind at all
(C) was so long that crews suffered scurvy without resupply
(D) was blocked by the Ottoman Empire's control of the sea route
explanation: The key is (C). A round trip to Asia took the better part of two years, and crews died of scurvy and starvation when fresh food and water ran out. The Cape station existed to break that deadly stretch: the painting's boats ferrying supplies to anchored ships show the remedy in action.

stem: Historians use advertisements like this one as evidence that
stimulus: A 1748 newspaper advertisement from the Pennsylvania Gazette: 'RUN away... from Philip Syng, of this city, silversmith, a Negroe man, named Cato, about 20 years old... speaks good English... had on when he went away two jackets...' The ad offers 'Twenty Shillings reward' for his return.
options: (A) enslaved people accepted slavery without any resistance
(B) enslaved people actively resisted bondage by running away
(C) colonial newspapers firmly opposed the institution of slavery
(D) rewards offered for runaways were never actually paid out
explanation: The key is (B). The advertisement exists because Cato escaped: a master would not pay for newspaper space and offer twenty shillings unless running away was a real, recurring threat. Thousands of such ads in colonial papers document the persistent, everyday resistance of enslaved people who seized their own freedom.

stem: The advertisement describes Cato as a silversmith's worker who 'speaks good English' and lists his clothing in detail. These details best show that
stimulus: A 1748 newspaper advertisement from the Pennsylvania Gazette: 'RUN away... from Philip Syng, of this city, silversmith, a Negroe man, named Cato, about 20 years old... speaks good English... had on when he went away two jackets...' The ad offers 'Twenty Shillings reward' for his return.
options: (A) Cato was a free white apprentice working for wages
(B) the master was concerned only for Cato's welfare and safety
(C) most enslaved people in Pennsylvania were field workers on large farms nearby
(D) enslaved people were treated as valuable property worth describing
explanation: The key is (D). The ad catalogs Cato the way one catalogs lost property: trade, language, age, clothing, all to identify and recover him. The careful description of a skilled, English-speaking worker shows enslaved people were valued assets, and the notice's purpose, to get the 'property' back, lays bare the property logic of slavery.

stem: The image best illustrates which aspect of early English-Indigenous contact in North America?
stimulus: A circa-1585 English watercolor titled 'Their sitting at meate,' by the artist John White, showing an Algonquian man in Virginia seated on a mat eating fish, with a pot, a gourd, and fish laid out beside him.
options: (A) English curiosity about Indigenous foodways and daily life
(B) large-scale English military conquest of Virginia in the year 1618
(C) Algonquian adoption of English farming methods and crops
(D) the complete absence of any contact before the year 1620
explanation: The key is (A). The watercolor carefully records what the man eats and the vessels he eats from: an ethnographic study, not a battle scene. In the fragile early years of Jamestown, colonists depended on Indigenous food and knowledge, and images like this show English observers documenting the daily life of the people whose world they had entered.

stem: A historian should interpret this image cautiously because it
stimulus: A circa-1585 English watercolor titled 'Their sitting at meate,' by the artist John White, showing an Algonquian man in Virginia seated on a mat eating fish, with a pot, a gourd, and fish laid out beside him.
options: (A) was painted centuries after the events that it depicts
(B) shows only landscapes with no people in them
(C) was made by an English observer for an English audience
(D) was created by the Algonquian man himself as a self-portrait
explanation: The key is (C). The watercolor was painted by an English colonist for readers back in England, who expected edifying curiosities from the New World. That purpose shaped the image: the Algonquian man is presented as a specimen of native life, posed and labeled for European consumption, so historians must read it as a European view of Indigenous people rather than an Indigenous self-portrait.

stem: The fort's design and buildings best indicate that Ouidah served as
stimulus: A 1747 French plan of the fort at Ouidah (in present-day Benin). It shows a square walled fort with bastions, cannons, a flag, and labeled buildings including storerooms, drawn with military precision.
options: (A) a French settler farming colony on the coast
(B) a fortified base for the slave trade, holding captives
(C) a missionary center with no military function at all
(D) an African-built fortress that excluded Europeans entirely
explanation: The key is (B). The plan shows a compact military installation: bastions, cannon, and storerooms, not farms or a town. Ouidah was one of the principal ports of the transatlantic slave trade, and the fort's purpose was to warehouse captive Africans and trade goods securely while French agents negotiated purchases with African rulers and awaited ships.

stem: European powers built forts like the one at Ouidah rather than simply anchoring offshore because they needed to
stimulus: A 1747 French plan of the fort at Ouidah (in present-day Benin). It shows a square walled fort with bastions, cannons, a flag, and labeled buildings including storerooms, drawn with military precision.
options: (A) grow food for the long voyage back to Europe
(B) house large European settler populations on the coast for farming tobacco
(C) escape taxation by their own governments back home
(D) defend stored captives and goods while keeping African rulers' favor
explanation: The key is (D). A ship at anchor could be attacked and could not store captives for months while awaiting the Middle Passage sailing season. The fort solved both problems: its cannons defended valuable human cargo and goods against rival Europeans, and its permanent presence embodied the negotiated agreements, rents, and customs paid to African rulers who controlled access to the trade.

stem: The engenho shown best exemplifies which feature of the Brazilian sugar economy?
stimulus: A seventeenth-century engraving by Georg Marcgraf of a Brazilian sugar mill (engenho). It shows cane fields, a water-powered mill building, boiling houses, storehouses, and the planter's house arranged as one complex.
options: (A) farming and industry combined in a single large enterprise
(B) small-scale peasant sugar farming in the interior
(C) the absence of water power in colonial industry entirely at the time
(D) sugar production carried out without enslaved labor
explanation: The key is (A). The engraving lays out the whole system in one view: fields feeding a water-powered crushing mill, boiling houses refining the juice, storehouses holding the product, and the big house overseeing all. The engenho was an agro-industrial complex where growing and manufacturing happened under one management, the characteristic unit of the sugar economy.

stem: Because sugar cane had to be crushed quickly after cutting and the equipment shown was expensive, sugar production tended to
stimulus: A seventeenth-century engraving by Georg Marcgraf of a Brazilian sugar mill (engenho). It shows cane fields, a water-powered mill building, boiling houses, storehouses, and the planter's house arranged as one complex.
options: (A) be done by independent small farmers on their own
(B) move away from the coast toward the interior
(C) concentrate land, capital, and enslaved labor in a few hands
(D) decline steadily in profitability over the course of the 1600s
explanation: The key is (C). Cane spoils within days of cutting, so planters needed their own mill, and mills cost a fortune to build and run. That technical and financial logic, visible in the engraving's integrated complex, drove consolidation: wealth concentrated in the few who could afford an engenho, worked by large enslaved crews on extensive lands.

stem: In the 1600s the Banda Islands were the world's only source of nutmeg. This fact best explains why the Dutch East India Company (VOC)
stimulus: A painting of nutmeg harvesters at work among the trees on Lontor, one of the tiny Banda Islands in eastern Indonesia. Workers gather the fruit beneath tall tropical trees.
options: (A) ignored the islands as commercially worthless specks
(B) used violence to monopolize the islands' nutmeg
(C) shared the nutmeg trade freely with the English merchants
(D) banned the consumption of nutmeg in Europe
explanation: The key is (B). Nutmeg sold in Europe for many times its Asian price, and the painting shows why it was so precious: it grew only in this one tiny archipelago. To capture those profits, the VOC conquered the Bandas in 1621, killed or enslaved much of the population, and enforced a monopoly that kept prices high for a century.

stem: The painting shows a small island grove producing a spice Europeans could not grow at home. This geographic reality best explains which pattern of the spice trade?
stimulus: A painting of nutmeg harvesters at work among the trees on Lontor, one of the tiny Banda Islands in eastern Indonesia. Workers gather the fruit beneath tall tropical trees.
options: (A) Spices were cheap and abundant for Europeans
(B) Europeans had no real demand for Asian goods
(C) The Dutch allowed free competition in the nutmeg trade there always
(D) Holding tiny island sources brought enormous profits and power
explanation: The key is (D). The image makes the economics visible: the entire world supply came from groves like this one on a speck of land. Whoever controlled that speck controlled the global supply, which is why a handful of islands could make the VOC rich and why Europeans fought wars over them.

stem: The imagery and motto on this coin best reflect which development?
stimulus: A Spanish silver coin dated 1759, an 'eight reales' piece (piece of eight). One face shows two crowned pillars wrapped in banners reading 'VTRAQUE VNUM' ('both are one') between the Pillars of Hercules, with the date 1759 below.
options: (A) American silver became a global currency joining Spain's two worlds
(B) Spain had abandoned all of its American colonies entirely by the year 1759
(C) the coin was used only within Spain itself, never abroad
(D) China refused to accept any foreign silver at all
explanation: The key is (A). The Pillars of Hercules stood for Spain's Old World realm and the New World beyond them; 'both are one' proclaimed their union. Struck from American silver in 1759, the piece of eight became the world's most widely circulated coin, accepted from the Americas to Asia: a global currency born of New World mines.

stem: Silver mined at Potosi was minted into coins like this one, which have been found by archaeologists from Mexico to the Philippines to China. This distribution best supports which conclusion?
stimulus: A Spanish silver coin dated 1759, an 'eight reales' piece (piece of eight). One face shows two crowned pillars wrapped in banners reading 'VTRAQUE VNUM' ('both are one') between the Pillars of Hercules, with the date 1759 below.
options: (A) Spain successfully kept all of its silver within its own empire
(B) the Chinese economy had no use for silver as money
(C) American silver fueled a global trade network feeding Chinese demand
(D) the Manila galleons carried only silk across the Pacific, never silver
explanation: The key is (C). The coin's travels trace the silver circuit: mined at Potosi, minted in Spanish America, shipped across the Pacific on the Manila galleons, and absorbed by China, whose tax system and economy ran on silver. The archaeological footprint of one coin type across three continents is the material record of the first truly global trade.

stem: Based on the image, which statement best explains what drove the crowd's attack on the Bastille?
stimulus: A line engraving of the storming of the Bastille, July 14, 1789: a dense crowd of armed men and women surges toward a stone fortress through clouds of smoke. Cannon fire erupts from the fortress walls while figures in the crowd haul a cannon forward and others wave flags and pikes. The scene shows open, chaotic street fighting between the crowd and the fortress's defenders.
options: (A) The crowd attacked because the king had ordered the fortress demolished as punishment for Paris's earlier riots, and the mob was merely carrying out his royal command.
(B) The crowd sought the fortress's stored gunpowder and weapons, and the attack became the violent symbol of popular revolt against royal authority.
(C) The crowd was a foreign army invading Paris to overthrow the French monarchy by force.
(D) The crowd attacked to free hundreds of political prisoners held inside the fortress dungeons.
explanation: The engraving shows an armed crowd fighting the fortress's defenders, with cannon and gunfire on both sides. The Bastille was attacked mainly for its gunpowder and arms, and July 14 became the revolution's founding symbol of popular violence toppling royal authority.

stem: What criticism of the Old Regime does this image express?
stimulus: An engraving titled 'Allegorie dediée au tiers état' (Allegory dedicated to the Third Estate): a peasant, labeled as the Third Estate, is bent double under the weight of two men he carries on his back — one labeled as the nobility and one as the clergy. The peasant strains forward while the two riders sit comfortably above him.
options: (A) The Third Estate bore the burden of taxation while the clergy and nobility were largely exempt, making the system unjust.
(B) The Third Estate enjoyed more political rights and privileges than the clergy and nobility combined.
(C) The image celebrates Napoleon's rise from the Third Estate to emperor of the French.
(D) The image shows that the trade guilds of Paris controlled the French economy and dictated tax policy to the king's ministers.
explanation: The bent peasant carrying the other two orders visualizes the fiscal injustice of the Old Regime: the Third Estate paid most taxes while the privileged orders were exempt — a central grievance behind 1789.

stem: What was the historical significance of the event depicted?
stimulus: Jacques-Louis David's large unfinished painting of the Tennis Court Oath, June 20, 1789: inside a crowded indoor tennis court, dozens of deputies stand with their right arms raised in unison toward the center, where the assembly's president, Bailly, stands on a table reading from a document. Light streams through high windows onto the raised arms of the crowd.
options: (A) The deputies swore an oath of personal loyalty to Louis XVI, promising to defend his absolute authority against all challengers and to uphold the traditional social hierarchy of the three estates.
(B) The deputies voted to have the king executed.
(C) The deputies of the Third Estate pledged not to disband until they had written a constitution, directly challenging the king's authority.
(D) The deputies declared war on Austria and Prussia.
explanation: Locked out of their meeting hall, the Third Estate's deputies swore the Tennis Court Oath not to separate until a constitution was written — the moment the revolution claimed sovereignty from the king.

stem: The principles proclaimed in this document drew most directly on which intellectual tradition?
stimulus: An engraved 1789 broadside of the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen: the text is set on two stone tablets framed by classical columns, with allegorical winged figures above and the heading addressed 'Aux représentants du peuple français' (to the representatives of the French people).
options: (A) Medieval Catholic theology on the divine right of kings to rule without any limits.
(B) The economic doctrines of mercantilism, which taught that national wealth came from favorable trade balances and the accumulation of gold and silver in state treasuries.
(C) Napoleon's military maxims on centralized command and battlefield discipline.
(D) Enlightenment natural-rights philosophy, which held that liberty, property, and resistance to oppression belong to all men and that law expresses the general will.
explanation: The Declaration's claims — liberty, property, legal equality, resistance to oppression, law as the general will — are textbook Enlightenment natural-rights ideas from thinkers like Locke, Montesquieu, and Rousseau.

stem: What does the wording of this preamble reveal about the author's purpose?
stimulus: The first page of Olympe de Gouges's 1791 pamphlet, 'Déclaration des droits de la femme et de la citoyenne.' Its preamble reads: 'Les mères, les filles, les soeurs, représentantes de la nation, demandent d'être constituées en assemblée nationale' (The mothers, daughters, and sisters, representatives of the nation, demand to be constituted as a national assembly).
options: (A) She opposed the French Revolution and wanted to restore the monarchy.
(B) She was turning the Revolution's own logic back on itself, demanding that the rights promised to 'men' in 1789 apply to women as well.
(C) She was defending the traditional exclusion of women from politics as natural and proper, arguing that women's place was in the home rather than in the assembly.
(D) She was announcing that women had already won the vote in 1791.
explanation: By mirroring the men's declaration — 'representatives of the nation' demanding a national assembly — de Gouges exposed the contradiction of a revolution proclaiming universal rights while excluding women.

stem: What major political change is reflected in this image?
stimulus: An engraving of the National Assembly in session on February 4, 1790: a large hall filled with rows of seated deputies facing a central rostrum where a speaker stands, with crowded public galleries above watching the proceedings.
options: (A) Sovereignty had shifted from the king ruling alone to a representative assembly claiming to speak for the nation.
(B) The king had personally appointed the deputies to advise him on financial matters, then dismissed them once they had approved his plan to raise new taxes.
(C) The assembly is shown voting by the three separate orders, as the Estates-General had traditionally done.
(D) The image shows Napoleon's coronation as emperor.
explanation: The National Assembly — the Third Estate's deputies joined by reformers from the other orders — governed France in the king's name, marking the transfer of sovereignty from monarch to nation.

stem: What does this image best illustrate about the Reign of Terror?
stimulus: A 1793 engraving of the execution of Charlotte Corday in the Place de la Révolution (now Place de la Concorde): a large crowd surrounds the scaffold where the guillotine stands; carts and armed guards manage the dense onlookers gathered to watch the execution of the woman who had assassinated the radical leader Marat.
options: (A) The guillotine was used only against members of the nobility.
(B) Charlotte Corday was executed for being a secret royalist agent who had plotted with emigres to assassinate the republic's leaders.
(C) The revolutionary government used public execution as a political weapon against anyone it defined as an enemy of the revolution.
(D) Public executions had been abolished after 1789.
explanation: Corday — a Girondin sympathizer, not a royalist — was guillotined before a mass audience. The Terror made exemplary public execution the state's tool against political enemies of every stripe.

stem: What does this British cartoon reveal about British attitudes toward the French Revolution in 1790?
stimulus: James Gillray's 1790 hand-colored cartoon 'Alecto and her train, at the gate of Pandaemonium': a monstrous fury labeled Alecto and a French drummer recruit a bewildered Englishman, 'John Bull,' into what the caption calls 'the Revolution Service,' while speech-filled papers swirl around them.
options: (A) Gillray supported the French Revolution and urged Britons to join it.
(B) The cartoon celebrates a new military alliance between Britain and revolutionary France against their common continental rivals in central and eastern Europe.
(C) The cartoon shows British troops preparing to invade France.
(D) Conservative Britons feared revolutionary ideas would cross the Channel, and the cartoon mocks British radicals as dupes being recruited by French monsters.
explanation: Gillray, a conservative satirist, portrays French revolutionaries as literal demons from hell (Pandaemonium) luring John Bull — propaganda expressing elite British fear of revolutionary contagion.

stem: What view of the Congress of Vienna does this cartoon express?
stimulus: An 1815 British cartoon, 'The bungling tinkers, or Congress of blockheads': bewigged diplomats hammer and patch a large cracked kettle labeled as Europe, while the caption jeers that they have 'battered a hole in great Europe's kettle.'
options: (A) The cartoonist saw the diplomats as clumsy elites botching the restoration of Europe's monarchies out of self-interest.
(B) The cartoonist praised the Congress for skillfully rebuilding Europe.
(C) The cartoon shows Napoleon himself directing the settlement while the allied diplomats merely watch, take notes, and carry out his personal instructions.
(D) The cartoon depicts the revolutions of 1848.
explanation: The 'bungling tinkers' metaphor — incompetent repairmen making the kettle worse — satirizes the Vienna diplomats as self-serving elites whose restoration settlement damaged Europe.

stem: Which criticism of the Vienna settlement is this caricature making?
stimulus: A French caricature captioned 'LE CONGRÈS': the great-power diplomats of the Congress of Vienna are drawn dancing together in a circle, arms linked, in festive dress, while Europe is rearranged around them.
options: (A) It celebrates the Congress for giving ordinary people the vote.
(B) It shows the diplomats as military commanders planning a war.
(C) It portrays the peacemakers as frivolous elites who redrew Europe's borders to suit monarchs while ignoring liberal and nationalist demands.
(D) It depicts the Frankfurt Parliament of 1848, where German liberals gathered after the March revolutions to draft a constitution for a united, democratic German nation-state.
explanation: The dancing circle mocks the diplomats as out-of-touch aristocrats waltzing while they restored monarchies and suppressed the nationalism and liberalism the revolutionary era had awakened.

stem: A historian studying the American Revolution finds this image. What is the most careful conclusion she can draw about its value as evidence?
stimulus: Emanuel Leutze's 1851 painting 'Washington Crossing the Delaware': George Washington stands upright in the prow of a crowded rowboat pushing through ice chunks on a dark river at dawn, an American flag streaming behind him while soldiers strain at the oars around him. The scene is dramatic, heroic, and carefully composed — painted 75 years after the 1776 event.
options: (A) It is a primary source painted by an eyewitness to the crossing.
(B) It is more useful as evidence of how 19th-century Americans remembered and mythologized the Revolution than as a record of the 1776 crossing itself.
(C) It shows Washington's defeat at the Battle of Trenton.
(D) It was commissioned by the British government to mock the American cause, discourage further rebellion in the colonies, and celebrate British military superiority.
explanation: Painted in 1851, the dramatic standing pose, flag, and dawn light are romantic invention, not documentation. The painting is excellent evidence of 19th-century nationalist memory — how Americans wanted to remember the founding — but weak evidence of the crossing itself.

stem: What does this image show about colonial resistance before 1776?
stimulus: A 19th-century print of the Boston Tea Party: under a moonlit sky, men in a harbor row alongside large sailing ships and heave wooden tea chests overboard into the water, where chests already float among the waves.
options: (A) The colonists were protesting a British ban on all tea imports that threatened the livelihoods of colonial merchants.
(B) The image shows a British naval victory over French ships.
(C) The protest was organized and funded by the British Parliament.
(D) Colonists destroyed tea cargo to protest Parliament's claim to tax them without their consent.
explanation: The tea destruction dramatized the colonists' refusal to pay Parliament's tea tax — property destruction as political protest against taxation without representation.

stem: What does the date and style of this engraving tell a historian about how to use it?
stimulus: An 1840 engraving by the American Bank Note Company titled 'Signing the declaration of their independence': in a formal, well-lit assembly room, bewigged men in 18th-century dress gather around a central table signing a large document, arranged in a balanced, almost theatrical composition.
options: (A) It is a 19th-century idealized commemoration, best used as evidence of how later Americans remembered the founding rather than of the 1776 event itself.
(B) It is a photograph taken during the signing in 1776.
(C) It proves that every signer shown was present in the room on July 4, 1776, signed the document on that exact day, and personally witnessed the final vote.
(D) It was printed and distributed in Philadelphia in 1776.
explanation: The 1840 engraving is a later commemoration — useful for studying 19th-century American memory of the founding, not the 1776 event's details.

stem: What does this portrait suggest about the social leadership of Latin American independence?
stimulus: José Gil de Castro's portrait of Simón Bolívar: Bolívar stands in full military dress — ornate gold-epauletted coat, white trousers, sword at his side — beneath a banner reading 'EL PERÚ RECONOCIDO A SIMÓN BOLÍVAR' (Peru grateful to Simón Bolívar), with a framed inscription below.
options: (A) Bolivar was an indigenous leader who rejected all European culture and military traditions, seeking instead to build a new state founded entirely on Native American customs and institutions.
(B) The portrait shows Bolivar as a loyal officer of the Spanish crown defending the empire.
(C) Bolivar was a creole elite whose military leadership of the independence wars reflects how American-born Spaniards, not the peninsulares, drove Spanish American independence.
(D) Bolivar opposed independence and fought to keep Peru under Spanish colonial rule.
explanation: Bolívar was a creole — American-born of Spanish descent — and creole elites led most Spanish American independence movements, seeking political power matching their economic status.

stem: Why is the battle shown here historically significant?
stimulus: An engraving of the Battle of Vertières, 1803: Black Haitian soldiers in military uniforms charge forward with muskets and bayonets against French troops, who fall back amid smoke and fallen bodies. The Haitian attackers advance in disciplined formation.
options: (A) The image shows a French victory that restored slavery in Saint-Domingue, ended the Haitian rebellion for good, and returned the colony to profitable plantation production.
(B) The image shows Haitian forces defeating the French army, the decisive victory that made Haiti the first independent Black republic founded by formerly enslaved people.
(C) The image shows a slave revolt being crushed by colonial militia.
(D) The image shows American troops aiding the French in Haiti.
explanation: At Vertières (1803) Dessalines's Black army defeated the French; Haiti's 1804 independence made it the first Black republic and the only successful revolution by enslaved people.

stem: What does this image demonstrate about how the Haitian Revolution was fought?
stimulus: Auguste Raffet's colored engraving of the combat and capture of Crête-à-Pierrot: Black Haitian soldiers swarm up a fortified hillside toward a French-held fort, firing muskets as French defenders resist; bodies lie on the slope beneath drifting smoke.
options: (A) Haitians won independence without any fighting.
(B) The image shows French colonists bravely defending their plantations against a disorganized mob of rebels with no military training or leadership.
(C) The image depicts a battle of the American Revolution.
(D) Formerly enslaved Haitians fought as organized armies using both conventional assaults and guerrilla tactics to defeat French forces.
explanation: Raffet shows Haitian troops as a real army storming fortifications — the revolution was waged by organized Black soldiers who defeated Europe's armies.

stem: What was the purpose of the expedition shown in this image?
stimulus: An engraving of the French fleet disembarking at Saint-Domingue in 1802: warships crowd the harbor while rowboats ferry uniformed French soldiers ashore amid cannon smoke, as the expedition moves against the colony's Black forces.
options: (A) Napoleon sent a French army to retake Saint-Domingue and restore slavery, which provoked the renewed war that ended in Haitian independence.
(B) The French fleet arrived to grant Saint-Domingue its independence peacefully.
(C) The image shows British troops landing to aid the Haitian rebels.
(D) The image depicts the American purchase of Louisiana from France in 1803, a peaceful diplomatic transaction negotiated by President Jefferson's envoys in Paris.
explanation: Napoleon dispatched General Leclerc's 1802 expedition to retake Saint-Domingue and restore slavery (abolished 1794). Toussaint's arrest and the war's renewal led directly to Haitian independence.

stem: What does this portrait reveal about Toussaint Louverture's historical role?
stimulus: An engraving labeled 'Toussaint L'Ouverture': a Black man in a French general's uniform with heavy epaulettes and a sash gazes directly at the viewer, his hand resting on his sword hilt.
options: (A) Toussaint was a French-born officer sent from Paris to govern the colony, suppress the slave rebellion there, and restore the plantation economy to full production under the old system.
(B) Toussaint opposed the abolition of slavery in Saint-Domingue.
(C) Toussaint rose from enslavement to command the colony's armies, and his European-style general's uniform projects his claim to legitimate authority.
(D) Toussaint was executed by the revolutionaries in 1791.
explanation: Born enslaved, Toussaint became the revolution's general and governor; the French-style uniform in his portrait asserts his status as a legitimate military and political leader.

stem: What is the artist communicating through the combination of European military dress and the tropical landscape?
stimulus: A 1806 engraving, 'Toussaint Louverture': a full-length portrait of a Black man in an ornate plumed hat, braided military coat, sash, and sword, holding official papers, with a tropical mountain landscape behind him and his name engraved below.
options: (A) It shows Toussaint wearing traditional African royal dress and ceremonial ornaments.
(B) The artist blends European symbols of military power with Toussaint's identity as a Black leader, projecting sovereignty to both European and Haitian viewers.
(C) It proves that Toussaint remained a loyal general serving Napoleon throughout his entire career, carrying out orders from Paris faithfully from his first commission to his final day.
(D) It is a British caricature mocking Toussaint's pretensions to grandeur and authority.
explanation: The 1806 print dresses the Black liberator in the full regalia of European power — plumed hat, sash, sword — while the tropical backdrop marks his Haitian domain: a visual argument that Black sovereignty deserved the same recognition as European states.

stem: What does this title page reveal about Napoleon's government?
stimulus: The title page of the 1804 'Code civil des Français': 'CODE CIVIL DES FRANÇAIS. ÉDITION ORIGINALE ET SEULE OFFICIELLE. À PARIS, DE L'IMPRIMERIE DE LA RÉPUBLIQUE. AN XII. — 1804,' beneath an allegorical female figure of Justice with scales.
options: (A) It restored feudal law and noble privilege.
(B) It was written before the French Revolution.
(C) It applied only within the city of Paris and was never enforced anywhere else in France or in the conquered satellite states of the Napoleonic empire at all.
(D) Napoleon's regime imposed a single uniform legal code, spreading legal equality and property rights while consolidating centralized authoritarian rule.
explanation: The Code civil standardized law across Napoleon's empire — equality before the law, property rights, religious toleration — while entrenching his authoritarian, patriarchal rule.

stem: Why was the machine shown here so important to industrialization?
stimulus: A labeled 1780 diagram of Watt's steam engine: a massive rocking beam connects a brick-encased boiler and piston on one side to a large flywheel on the other, with rods, valves, and a governor drawn in careful engineering detail.
options: (A) Steam power freed factories from rivers, so industry could locate near coal and labor and operate year-round, making the factory system possible.
(B) It was the very first machine ever invented by humans in all of recorded history, with no earlier mechanical devices of any kind whatsoever existing before it.
(C) It was powered by electricity.
(D) In 1780 it was used mainly to pull railroad trains.
explanation: Watt's efficient engine decoupled industry from rivers: factories could be built near coal, labor, and markets, run all year, and power many machines — the core of the factory system.

stem: What economic change does this machine best illustrate?
stimulus: An 1836 Penny Magazine engraving of Hargreaves's spinning jenny: a long wooden frame holds rows of upright spindles, turned by a single large wheel at one end, with a moving carriage — one operator could work many spindles simultaneously.
options: (A) It was powered by a steam engine from the day it was invented.
(B) It reduced the amount of raw cotton textile makers needed.
(C) It let one worker spin many threads at once, multiplying output per worker and pulling textile production from cottages into factories.
(D) It was invented in the 1760s to manufacture heavy canvas sails for the warships of the British Royal Navy during its naval arms race with France.
explanation: The jenny's many spindles let one worker spin many threads at once — productivity per worker soared, drawing textile work out of cottages into factories.

stem: What was the most important economic effect of the development shown here?
